title: What Is Linux? — Kernel, Distribution, Philosophy
lead: Understand what Linux really is: a kernel, the distributions built around it, and the ideas that make the command line so powerful.
objectives: You can explain the difference between the kernel, a distribution and the shell.
You know the two big distribution families (Debian and RHEL) and their package tools.
You find kernel version, distribution and architecture with `uname` and `/etc/os-release`.
You know the principle "everything is a file" and the purpose of the main top-level directories.

sections.title: Kernel, distribution and shell
body: **Linux** is strictly only the **kernel**: the core that talks to the hardware, schedules processes and manages memory. Linus Torvalds started it in 1991. Alone the kernel is not usable — you need tools, libraries and a way to type commands.

A **distribution** (distro) bundles the kernel with the GNU tools, a package manager, an installer and defaults. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux are distros. The **shell** (usually `bash`) is the program that reads your commands and asks the kernel to run them.
Two files tell you what you are running: `uname` reports kernel and architecture, `/etc/os-release` reports the distribution. You will use both whenever you ask for help or read documentation.

commands.where: When checking the kernel version for support or bug reports.
commands.why: The kernel version decides which hardware and features you have.

commands.what: Prints all system information in one line.
commands.where: When you paste system details into a ticket.
commands.why: Shows host name, kernel and architecture at once.

commands.where: Before downloading software or an ISO.

commands.why: A standard file, same format on Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma and others.

sections.tip: Kernel and distribution are versioned separately: Ubuntu 24.04 ships kernel 6.8, Rocky Linux 9 ships 5.14 with many backports.

sections.title: Distribution families and licences
body: Distros group into **families**. The **Debian family** (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint) uses `.deb` packages and `apt`. The **RHEL family** (Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Fedora) uses `.rpm` packages and `dnf`. Commands you learn in this course work on both; only package management differs.

The Linux kernel is released under GPL-2.0-only; tools and applications bundled in a distribution may use different licences. This openness supports many distros, while enterprise vendors may offer support and services as well as software. The `ID_LIKE` line in `/etc/os-release` tells you the family: Rocky reports `rhel fedora`, Ubuntu reports `debian`.
In this course your reference system is a **Rocky/Alma Linux** VM, with Ubuntu as an equal alternative. Use whichever you installed in module 0.2.

commands.what: Shows only the family line of the release file.
commands.where: When you are unsure whether to use apt or dnf.
commands.why: Turns a long file into the one fact you need.

sections.tip: If `ID_LIKE` contains `debian` use `apt`; if it contains `rhel` or `fedora` use `dnf`.

sections.title: Philosophy and the directory tree
body: Unix thinking in four lines: **everything is a file** (disks, devices and processes show up as paths), **small tools do one thing well**, tools are **combined** with pipes, and configuration is **plain text** you can read and edit.

All files live in **one tree** starting at `/` (root directory). There are no drive letters. `/etc` holds configuration, `/home` the users' files, `/var` changing data such as logs, `/usr` programs and libraries, `/tmp` temporary files, `/dev` devices, `/proc` live kernel information. On modern systems `/bin` is just a link to `/usr/bin`.
A normal user works in the home directory `/home/student`. The administrator account is **root**; you will meet it carefully in later modules.

commands.what: Lists the top level of the directory tree.
commands.where: When getting oriented on an unknown system.
commands.why: Shows the standard directories described above.

commands.where: When looking for a system setting.
commands.why: Nearly all system configuration is a text file here.

commands.what: Lists the shells installed on the system.
commands.where: When asking which shell programs exist.
commands.why: Shows that the shell is just a replaceable program.

sections.tip: When something is configurable, look in `/etc` first, then read the file — it is text.

t04.text: List the top level of the directory tree with `ls /`.

t07.text: Predict: which architecture will `uname -m` print on this system? Then run it.
t07.hint: Most PCs and VMs use x86_64.

t08.text: Predict: what does `cat /etc/hostname` contain? Run it to check.

t09.text: Predict: what does `echo $SHELL` print? Run it to check.
t09.hint: It is the full path to your shell program.

t10.text: Debug: `~/distro.txt` wrongly says `ID=windows`. Overwrite the file so that it contains `ID=linux`.
t10.hint: `echo ID=linux > ~/distro.txt` replaces the content; check with `cat`.

t11.text: Mini project: create the folder `~/about_linux`. Save the kernel release in `~/about_linux/kernel.txt` and the contents of `/etc/os-release` in `~/about_linux/distro.txt`.
t11.hint: `uname -r > file` writes command output into a file.

t12.text: Challenge: build `~/system_report.txt` with three lines: host name, kernel release and your user name.

t13.text: Ticket: "A colleague asks which distribution family this server belongs to. Save the `ID_LIKE` line of the release file in `~/ticket_answer.txt`."
t13.hint: Combine `grep` for the line with `>` for the file.

vm.intro: These commands are harmless and read-only. Run them in the terminal of your VM (Rocky/Alma or Ubuntu) and compare.

v01.title: Identify your system
v01.text: Show kernel release and distribution, and paste both outputs.

blocks.expected:
5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64
NAME="Rocky Linux"
VERSION="9.4 (Blue Onyx)"
ID="rocky"
ID_LIKE="rhel centos fedora"
...

differs: On Ubuntu you see `NAME="Ubuntu"` and a kernel like `6.8.0-...-generic` — that is correct.
On WSL the kernel name contains `microsoft-standard-WSL2`.

v02.title: Walk the directory tree
v02.text: List the top level and the configuration directory and paste the output of the first command.

blocks.expected: afs  bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  lib64  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var

differs: The exact list varies by distribution, but `etc`, `home`, `usr` and `var` must be present.
`bin` appears as a link to `usr/bin` on modern systems; check with `ls -ld /bin`.

v03.title: Meet process 1
v03.text: Every system starts one first process. Find out its name.
differs: In some containers you may see `bash` or `init`; on a normal VM it is `systemd`.

v04.title: Check the link and your family
v04.text: Check that `/bin` is a link and decide whether your system uses apt or dnf.

blocks.cmd:
ls -ld /bin
grep ID_LIKE /etc/os-release
which apt dnf

differs: `which` prints only the tool that exists: `apt` on Ubuntu, `dnf` on Rocky/Alma.
If `which` prints nothing for both, try `command -v dnf` or install `which` first.

options: A complete operating system with desktop
The core that manages hardware, memory and processes
q1.explain: Linux strictly means the kernel. A distribution adds tools, packages and an installer around it.

q2.q: Which package tool belongs to the Rocky Linux / RHEL family?
q2.explain: RHEL-family systems use rpm packages managed by dnf; Debian and Ubuntu use apt.

q3.q: Which file shows the name and version of the distribution?
q3.explain: `/etc/os-release` is the standard file on all modern distributions.

q4.q: What does "everything is a file" mean?
options: Devices, processes and settings are reached through paths and read with the same tools
q4.explain: Disks appear under `/dev` and processes under `/proc`; the same tools such as `cat` and `ls` work on them.

summary: Linux is the kernel; a distribution adds tools, packages and an installer; the shell reads your commands.
Debian family uses `apt`, RHEL family uses `dnf`; `ID_LIKE` in `/etc/os-release` tells you which.
One tree from `/`: `/etc` configuration, `/home` users, `/var` data, `/usr` programs.
Unix philosophy: everything is a file, small tools, plain text configuration.

glossary.meaning: The core of the operating system that controls hardware, memory and processes.
A complete system: kernel plus tools, packages, installer and defaults.
The program that reads and runs your commands, usually bash.
The tool that installs and updates software: apt or dnf.
The top of the file tree, written `/`.
A family of free-software licences; the Linux kernel is licensed under GPL-2.0-only.
